title: Cortical Mastoidectomy for Acute Mastoiditis / Subperiosteal Abscess
source_label: Pasha 6e and Cummings 7e (Complications of Temporal Bone Infections; Mastoidectomy)
indications: Acute coalescent mastoiditis on CT (loss of bony septations, cortical erosion), subperiosteal abscess (postauricular, Bezold at the SCM insertion, Citelli in the digastric groove, Luc at the zygomatic root), failure to improve after 24-48 hours of parenteral antibiotics and myringotomy, or intratemporal or intracranial complications (facial palsy, labyrinthitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, epidural or brain abscess, meningitis). Noncoalescent mastoiditis is managed first with IV antibiotics and myringotomy with or without a tube. Many uncomplicated pediatric subperiosteal abscesses can be managed with myringotomy and tube plus incision and drainage or needle aspiration, reserving mastoidectomy for nonresponders or coalescence. Coordinate with neurosurgery and pediatrics when intracranial disease is present.
setup: Contrast CT temporal bone and, if intracranial complication or sigmoid thrombosis suspected, MRI/MRV; review tegmen, sigmoid position and any dehiscence
General anesthesia, supine, head turned, no long-acting paralysis after induction so facial nerve monitoring is reliable
Facial nerve monitor, otologic drill with cutting and diamond burrs, suction irrigation, operating microscope
Myringotomy blade and tympanostomy tubes; culture swabs and anaerobic transport
Plan with infectious disease for culture-directed IV therapy; neurosurgery available if intracranial extension
landmarks: Henle spine and suprameatal triangle (Macewen triangle)
Sigmoid sinus plate and sinodural angle
Mastoid antrum and lateral semicircular canal
Short process of incus in the fossa incudis
Digastric ridge (facial nerve exits anterior to it)
danger: Facial nerve (especially in children with a shallow, laterally placed mastoid tip and stylomastoid foramen)
Sigmoid sinus and emissary veins, which may be thrombosed or dehiscent
Tegmen dura with possible epidural abscess
Incus (avoid drilling contact in the aditus)
steps: Myringotomy first

Under the microscope, perform an anteroinferior myringotomy, aspirate and send middle ear fluid for aerobic, anaerobic and fungal culture, and place a tympanostomy tube. This drains the middle ear and provides a path for topical therapy after surgery.
Postauricular incision

Make a curvilinear incision about 1 cm behind the postauricular crease. In infants, keep it more posterior and shallow because the mastoid tip is undeveloped and the facial nerve exits superficially. If a subperiosteal abscess is present, expect pus immediately beneath the soft tissue.
Drain the abscess

Open the abscess cavity, culture the pus, and irrigate. Raise a periosteal flap (Palva or T-shaped) to expose the mastoid cortex. Look for a cortical fistula or necrotic bone indicating the route of spread, often near the spine of Henle.
Identify surface landmarks

Expose the spine of Henle, temporal line and mastoid tip. The suprameatal triangle overlies the antrum. Inflamed periosteum and granulation can obscure landmarks, so clear soft tissue methodically before drilling.
Begin cortical drilling

With a large cutting burr and continuous suction irrigation, saucerize the cortex starting along the temporal line and parallel to the posterior canal wall, defining the tegmen superiorly and the sigmoid posteriorly. Use broad strokes, staying wide rather than deep.
Remove infected air cells

Remove coalesced cells and granulation tissue from the mastoid with burrs and curettes, sending tissue for culture and pathology. Bleeding granulation is common; use a diamond burr and gentle pressure near the sigmoid and tegmen.
Open the antrum

Follow the tegmen medially to enter the antrum, identifying the lateral semicircular canal and short process of incus. Establish patency of the aditus to allow communication with the middle ear. A canal wall up cortical mastoidectomy is the goal; facial recess opening is not required.
Assess the sigmoid and tegmen

Inspect the sigmoid plate for perisinus abscess or granulation and the tegmen for epidural abscess. If sinus thrombosis is present, decompress the sinus and drain perisinus pus; needle aspiration or opening the sinus is individualized and coordinated with the team.
Irrigate and decide drainage

Irrigate the cavity copiously. Place a small drain or wick through the wound when there was a large abscess cavity, or close primarily over a clean cavity. Ensure no residual pus pockets in tip cells or the zygomatic root.
Close

Replace the periosteal flap and close in layers. Apply a mastoid dressing. Send all specimens labeled, including for cholesteatoma pathology if unexpected keratin was found, which would change the operative plan.
exit_check: Antrum opened and aditus patent; coalescent cells and abscess fully drained
Facial nerve stimulates at low threshold and sigmoid and tegmen intact or addressed
Tube in place and cultures sent from middle ear, abscess and bone
postop: Culture-directed parenteral antibiotics with transition to oral therapy guided by clinical response and infectious disease input
Ototopical drops through the tube; mastoid dressing removed at 24-48 hours
Monitor facial function, fever curve, headache, and neurologic status
Anticoagulation decision for sigmoid thrombosis with neurology/hematology
Audiogram once the ear has healed

early: Sigmoid sinus bleeding or air embolism
late: Conductive hearing loss or ossicular injury

attending_followup: What CT finding defines coalescent mastoiditis?

Loss of bony septations between air cells with coalescence into a single cavity, often with cortical erosion. Fluid in an intact mastoid alone is not coalescent mastoiditis and is common in routine otitis media.
Name the extratemporal abscesses by location.
Postauricular (most common), Bezold beneath the SCM from tip erosion, Citelli along the digastric groove, and Luc beneath the temporalis from the zygomatic root or canal.
Otorrhea, abducens palsy from Dorello canal involvement and retro-orbital pain, indicating petrous apicitis.
Why is the facial nerve at greater risk in infants?
The mastoid tip is undeveloped until about age 2, so the stylomastoid foramen and nerve lie superficial and lateral near a standard postauricular incision.
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus, with Fusobacterium in anaerobic and sinus thrombosis cases.
